doc: The live-ETA protocol rules (WP5-1): what a frame means, what a client does with one, which targets can be watched, how fast a shard polls, how long a client waits before reconnecting, which shard owns a target set, and how a socket URL is derived. Two things make this corpus different from the others in this package. First, several of these rules run in TWO runtimes — `diffEtas` builds the `delta` the Durable Object sends AND the one the polling emulator synthesises from two HTTP fetches; `acceptTargets` decides the accepted set on both sides — so a port that disagrees here does not merely render differently, it emits different frames. Second, every list these rules return is canonically ordered by `(stopId, routeId)`, with exactly one documented exception (`applyLiveEtasToNearby`, which is soonest-first because a card truncates); without a total order the socket engine and the polling engine produce the same data in two orders and the wave's byte-identity acceptance cannot be met by any implementation. Timestamps in these rows are verbatim in the two formats the wire really uses: `+08:00` from the operators, `Z`-suffixed UTC where our own layer stamped it. Third — added after review — two of these rules are here because they were *not*: a session's accepted target set (`applyLiveFrame` dropped `SnapshotFrame.targets`, so no platform could perform the comparison the field is published for) and the reconnect schedule (`liveReconnectDelayMs`, which lived in the client layer while the socket port named iOS and Android as its implementations). Both are the same species: a rule three platforms would each have had to reinvent, in the one function they hand-port.

sameReading.doc: Is a second reading of the same route-at-stop *news*? Every field of `Eta` is compared except `observedAt`. That single exclusion is what makes a delta protocol worth having: `observedAt` records when we fetched a reading, so it moves on every poll round, and a port that compared it would report every reading as changed every round — a `delta` frame that is a `snapshot` with extra steps, and a screen that repaints continuously. A port that compared *too few* fields is the opposite failure and just as silent: the bus moves and nothing repaints.

cases.name: identical-readings-are-not-news
cases.why: The control. Also the only row that exercises every field comparison in one call — if a port compares fields lazily and this row is its only passing one, the rows below will say so.

cases.name: only-observedat-differs
cases.why: THE load-bearing row. Two poll rounds a minute apart returning the identical operator reading. `observedAt` differs by construction; the reading is not news. Compare it and every round becomes a full repaint, which defeats the entire protocol.

cases.name: an-arrival-time-moved
cases.why: The ordinary update: the bus is now due a minute later. Both readings carry an identical destination, which is also the only row where `sameText` compares two *present* values and finds them equal.

cases.name: an-arrival-was-added
cases.why: A third arrival appeared. Lengths differ, so a port comparing element-wise must check the length first or it reads past the end of the shorter list.

cases.name: arrivals-reordered
cases.why: Same two times, swapped. `arrivals` is soonest-first and the order is the data, so this is a different reading — a port that compared the two lists as sets would call it unchanged and leave the wrong bus at the top of the card.

cases.name: the-operator-republished-the-same-arrivals
cases.why: `dataTimestamp` moved but the arrival times did not. This IS news, and the reason is `isStale`: it ages a reading by `dataTimestamp`, so withholding the new timestamp would leave the client marking a freshly confirmed reading as stale. Upstream republishes about once a minute, so this is a common round, not an exotic one.

cases.name: a-different-route-at-the-same-stop
cases.why: Not the same reading at all. Included because `diffEtas` keys on the pair and a comparison that ignored `routeId` would let one route's reading overwrite another's.

cases.name: the-same-route-at-another-pole
cases.why: One route serves both kerbs of a merged place (ADR-042) and each pole has its own arrival times. A comparison that ignored `stopId` would collapse them.

cases.name: the-operator-code-changed
cases.why: KMB and LWB share route numbers on joint services, so the operator is part of what a reading is — and it is what decides the livery a card is drawn in.

cases.name: a-fare-appeared
cases.why: Absent versus present, on an optional field. A port that compared with `??` or a truthiness test would treat an appearing fare as no change and never show it.

cases.name: the-fare-changed
cases.why: Sectional fares change when the dataset is rebuilt. A decimal STRING — compared as text, never parsed to a float.

cases.name: a-destination-appeared
cases.why: The absent-versus-present case for localized text. `sameText` must distinguish absent from present, which is not the same comparison as comparing two present values.

cases.name: the-destination-differs-in-one-locale-only
cases.why: Identical `en`, different `zh-Hans`. A port that compared only the active locale — or only `en`, which is the tempting shortcut — would leave a Chinese-locale rider looking at a stale destination for ever.

cases.name: a-blank-english-destination-is-still-a-destination
cases.why: Upstream really does send an empty `en` (this package carries required corpus rows for it elsewhere). Absent and present-but-blank are different readings, so a port that folded `''` into absence would miss the change.

cases.name: a-remark-appeared
cases.why: A 'Scheduled' remark appearing turns a live reading into a lower-confidence one — the honesty cue ADR-008 exists for. Missing this change would present a timetable guess as a tracked bus.

cases.name: remarkkind-appeared-without-the-remark-text-changing
cases.why: The absent-versus-"info" trap the wire contract warns about, as a change. The server classifies the remark it already sent; the class is a separate field and must be compared separately or the tone the row renders in never updates.

diffEtas.doc: The one declaration of *what changed*, called by both engines: the `EtaHub` Durable Object builds the `delta` it sends with it, and the polling emulator builds the identical frame from two successive HTTP fetches. That shared use is what makes the two transports comparable at all, so these rows are a specification of the frame, not just of a function. `gone` is not an optimisation — polling replaces the whole payload so a departed bus vanishes for free, while a delta stream without `gone` strands its last reading on screen for ever. Both output lists are canonically ordered by `(stopId, routeId)`, never by input order or arrival time.

cases.name: nothing-to-nothing
cases.why: The empty round. An alarm that fires against a stop with no service must produce an empty delta, not a null one — the caller decides whether an empty delta is worth sending, and it cannot decide that if this throws or returns nothing.

cases.name: the-first-round-reports-everything-as-changed
cases.why: There is no previous state, so every reading is new. This is also how a shard that just woke from hibernation behaves: hibernation discards in-memory state, so its `prev` is whatever it persisted — and if it persisted nothing, this row is the shape of its first delta.

cases.name: an-unchanged-round-reports-nothing
cases.why: The round that justifies the design. Same readings, new `observedAt` — nothing is news, so the frame is empty and the screen does not repaint. A port comparing `observedAt` produces a full delta here, every round, for ever.

cases.name: one-reading-moved-and-the-other-did-not
cases.why: The ordinary round: one route's arrivals shifted, the other's did not. Only the changed one is sent, which is the whole bandwidth argument — and the unchanged one must NOT be sent, or the client repaints a row that did not move.

cases.name: a-departed-bus-is-gone-not-merely-unchanged
cases.why: Upstream stopped listing the route: the bus has gone. Without `gone` the client keeps showing its last reading, ageing silently — the dishonesty ADR-008 forbids, and the one failure polling could never have.

cases.name: a-route-appears-mid-session
cases.why: A route with no reading a minute ago now has one — a first departure, or a bus that just entered the feed. New keys are `changed`, not a separate 'added' list: a client that merges by identity needs no distinction, and inventing one would be a third list for both engines to get wrong.

cases.name: changed-is-ordered-by-stop-then-route-not-by-arrival-time
cases.why: THE canonical-order row. The readings are handed over soonest-first — which is the order `/v1/nearby` serves and therefore the order the poll emulator sees — and come back ordered by `(stopId, routeId)`. Without this the socket and the poll emulator produce the same data in two orders and WP5-1's byte-identity acceptance is unmeetable by any implementation.

cases.name: gone-is-ordered-the-same-way
cases.why: The same total order on the `gone` list. Pinned separately because it is a list of `EtaRef`, not of `Eta`, and a port could easily sort one and not the other — which is a byte difference in a frame and nothing else.

cases.name: a-pair-repeated-in-one-round-keeps-the-last
cases.why: A server that fans out per pole can list the same route-at-stop twice — a place whose member pole is also watched directly. The later statement wins, and exactly one reading is reported, because two readings of one identity in one frame would leave the receiver's merge order deciding what it shows.

cases.name: the-same-route-at-two-poles-is-two-readings
cases.why: A merged place's two kerbs, one route number. The identity is the pair, so both survive; keying on `routeId` alone would silently drop one kerb's bus.

retainFailedPoles.doc: This round's readings, with the poles we could not ask about kept rather than dropped (ADR-073). The second rule in this module that runs in TWO runtimes: the poll emulator applies it to what `/v1/etas/:id` answered, and the `EtaHub` Durable Object applies it to what its own round read, so a hand-port that gets it wrong on one side produces a screen that blanks during an upstream outage on that platform only. The rule it completes is *a failed round is not a departure*, which both engines already held per **target** and neither held per **pole** — a place is N boarding points (ADR-042) and an upstream board call is per point, so an outage at one kerb of a two-kerb place arrived as a successful, partially empty answer. `next` always wins over a retained reading, a retained reading keeps its own timestamps so `isStale` can age it, and nothing is resurrected: only what `prev` already held can survive.

cases.name: no-failure-is-this-rounds-truth
cases.why: THE CONTROL. With nothing in `failedStopIds` the answer is exactly `next`, canonically ordered — no retention, no carry-over. Without this row an implementation that retained unconditionally would satisfy every other case here, and it would freeze a screen on the last reading it ever saw.

cases.name: a-pole-that-answered-reports-its-departure
cases.why: THE SECOND CONTROL, and the one that keeps the rule honest in the other direction. Identical to the row above and to the row below in every respect except which list the pole is in: the pole answered, it no longer lists 49X, so 49X has genuinely departed and must NOT be retained. `gone` exists for exactly this and ADR-008 forbids leaving a stale time on screen.

cases.name: a-failed-poles-readings-survive-the-round
cases.why: The rule itself: *a failed round is not a departure*. The board refused, so `next` carries nothing from this pole — and reporting that as a departure would tell the rider the bus had left when all that happened is that we could not ask. Before ADR-073 the edge could not even say this had happened: `coalesce` resolved a rejected board to `[]` and the call succeeded empty.

cases.name: a-fresh-reading-beats-a-retained-one
cases.why: A pole can fail *partway*: Citybus has no stop board, so a place is one upstream call per (pole, route), and one route can refuse while its neighbours answer. The pole is therefore named in `failedStopIds` while `next` still carries some of its readings — and the fresh 86K must win over the retained one. An implementation that indexed `prev` last would show a rider the older of two times it holds.

cases.name: a-retained-reading-keeps-its-own-timestamps
cases.why: Retention is not a refresh. `dataTimestamp` stays at the operator clock it was published with, so `isStale` ages it honestly (ADR-008) and the screen labels it rather than presenting a two-minute-old time as new. Stated as its own row because the tempting implementation — rebuild the reading with this round’s `observedAt` — passes every other case and defeats the one honesty cue a rider has.

cases.name: a-first-round-failure-retains-nothing
cases.why: There is nothing to keep. A subscription whose very first round met an outage has no previous readings, so this returns empty rather than inventing a state — which is what lets both engines suppress the snapshot entirely for that round (ADR-056 decision 14) instead of publishing `snapshot { etas: [] }`, the frame that means *this stop has no arrivals*.

cases.name: a-failed-pole-we-never-had-a-reading-for-adds-nothing
cases.why: The pole is in `failedStopIds` and `prev` holds nothing from it — a route that had no bus due before the outage started. Nothing is fabricated. The neighbouring pole’s reading is untouched, which is what makes this different from the first-round row above.

cases.name: a-place-id-in-the-failed-list-matches-no-reading
cases.why: BOUNDARY. `failedStopIds` names *poles*, because a pole is what an upstream board call is for. A caller that passed a merged `P:` place id gets no retention rather than a parse error or a wildcard match — the safe direction, and one an implementation that tried to be clever about place membership would get wrong. `Eta.stopId` is never a place id (the schema says so), so equality is the whole rule.

cases.name: one-line-at-two-poles-one-kerb-fails
cases.why: THE NAMED BOUNDARY ROW, and it is where WP5-9 and ADR-073 meet. Since ADR-072 an arrival is a line at a *kerb*, so 68K at Fu Kin Street is two readings under one place and a rider sees a row per kerb. When one kerb’s board refuses and the other answers, the two rules have to point in opposite directions in a single round: the answering kerb’s 68K genuinely departed and must go, the refusing kerb’s must stay. Collapse this to one reading per line — the model this repo had until 2026-07-31 — and there is no answer that is right for both kerbs.

cases.name: the-result-is-canonically-ordered
cases.why: D1: every list this module returns is sorted by `(stopId, routeId)` in code-point order, and this one is a union of two sources that arrive in different orders. Both engines feed the result straight into `diffEtas` and into a `snapshot`, so an order that depended on which readings happened to be retained would make the poll emulator and the shard emit different frames for identical data — the one property the scenario corpus exists to assert.

applyLiveFrame.doc: The whole client half of the protocol, as one pure reducer over `{ seq, etas, status }`. Two asymmetries are the substance of it and both are deliberate: a `snapshot` applies whatever `seq` it carries (it is the recovery path — refusing an 'old' one would make recovery unreachable exactly when a shard has restarted), while a `delta` at or below the current `seq` is ignored *and* asks for a resync (on an ordered transport a repeated counter means a different producer, not a late frame). Everything the reducer returns is canonically ordered, which is what makes a socket and the poll emulator produce identical listener output. `resyncNeeded` is reported, never thrown: a frame that arrives out of order still carries real data, and discarding it would leave the screen further behind than the data just handed to us. A third asymmetry, no less deliberate: **only a `snapshot` restates the accepted target set**, and every other frame carries the session's own through untouched. That field is the sole signal either producer sends for a target it refused, so a port that drops it shows a rider 'no buses due' for a stop nobody is watching — see `a-snapshot-echoes-the-accepted-target-set`.

cases.name: the-first-snapshot
cases.why: The ordinary start: nothing applied yet, and a snapshot at seq 1 establishes both the readings and the counter.

cases.name: a-snapshot-replaces-it-does-not-merge
cases.why: A reading the snapshot omits is gone, not retained. A port that merged a snapshot the way it merges a delta would strand departed buses on screen for the life of the session — with nothing to notice it, because the merge always looks plausible.

cases.name: a-snapshots-readings-are-canonically-ordered-however-they-arrive
cases.why: The server already sends them in order, so this row exists for the case where it does not — a shard bug, or a hand-written test fake. The reducer's output order must not depend on its input's, or the two transports diverge the first time one of them is wrong.

cases.name: a-snapshot-with-a-lower-seq-still-applies
cases.why: The recovery row. The shard restarted and its counter began again at 1 while we were at 12. Ignoring it on `seq` grounds — which is right for a delta — would wedge the session for ever with no error anywhere.

cases.name: a-snapshot-does-not-touch-status
cases.why: Data and connection state are separate frames for a reason: a client that is reconnecting keeps its honest label while its readings are replaced. Only a `status` frame moves `status`.

cases.name: a-snapshot-echoes-the-accepted-target-set
cases.why: **The row the discarded echo needed and did not have.** The client asked for two poles and the server now accepts one — a favourite saved under a pre-ADR-062 id, or a shard that dropped it — so the snapshot's `targets` is a strict subset of what was sent. `SnapshotFrame.targets` exists to be compared with what was asked for and both producers deliberately send no other signal, so a reducer that drops the field leaves every platform unable to perform the one comparison the field is for: the rider is shown 'no buses due' for a stop nobody is watching, which is the silent filter ADR-008 rules out. The subset is what makes the row bite — a port that echoed the *asked-for* set, or that rebuilt it with its own `acceptTargets`, passes a row where the two happen to be equal.

cases.name: the-next-delta-merges-and-advances-the-counter
cases.why: The everyday frame: one reading moved, the other did not, and `seq` advances by one. The unchanged reading must survive untouched — a merge that rebuilt the list from `changed` alone would blank every quiet route.

cases.name: a-delta-honours-gone
cases.why: The other half of D2. The departed reading is removed rather than left to age. A port that ignored `gone` passes every other row in this group.

cases.name: a-delta-that-both-changes-and-removes
cases.why: The realistic frame — one bus arrived and left the feed while another's time moved. Order matters within the merge only if a reading appears in both lists, which a correct shard never sends; this row pins the ordinary case so the two engines agree.

cases.name: a-delta-with-a-gap-applies-and-asks-for-a-resync
cases.why: We are at 3 and frame 5 arrives, so frame 4 is lost. Apply what we were given — it is real, current data — and tell the caller to fetch a fresh snapshot. Dropping the frame as well as the gap would leave the screen further behind than it needs to be.

cases.name: a-delta-before-any-snapshot-applies-and-asks-for-a-resync
cases.why: `seq: 0` is the client's 'nothing applied yet' sentinel and the wire's counter starts at 1, so a delta at seq 1 is arithmetically 'the next frame' and still leaves us with a state built from a description of change rather than from a truth. Hence applied AND resyncNeeded — the one row where those two coincide without a gap.

cases.name: a-repeated-delta-is-ignored-and-asks-for-a-resync
cases.why: The same `seq` twice. On an ordered transport that is not a late frame — it is two producers' frames interleaved, or a shard that restarted its counter. The state is left exactly as it was and the caller is told to resync, which is the decision this brief did not settle: 'ignore and carry on' would wedge the session silently.

cases.name: a-delta-from-a-restarted-shard-is-ignored-and-asks-for-a-resync
cases.why: Counter went backwards. Same treatment as the repeat, and pinned separately because a port writing `seq === state.seq` instead of `seq <= state.seq` passes the row above and fails this one — after which every frame from the new producer is applied out of order.

cases.name: gone-for-a-reading-we-never-had-is-not-an-error
cases.why: Ordinary after a resync, or when a delta crosses a snapshot. Removing something absent is a no-op, not a fault: throwing here would turn a benign race into a broken screen.

cases.name: a-status-frame-updates-status-and-nothing-else
cases.why: `seq` and `etas` are untouched — including `seq`, which a port might be tempted to advance because the frame arrived. A status frame carries no `seq` at all; advancing anything here would make the next real delta look like a gap.

cases.name: a-status-frame-carrying-a-failure
cases.why: The whole point of `WireError` travelling on the socket: the client can say *why* it is retrying, and `retryable` tells a background client whether to keep asking. Same shape as the HTTP envelope's, because it is the same declaration.

cases.name: a-status-frame-without-an-error-clears-the-previous-one
cases.why: Recovery. The status is replaced, not merged, so a stale failure cannot outlive the state that caused it — a port that spread the new state over the old would leave a 'timed out' error attached to a healthy connection, and some renderer would show it.

cases.name: a-status-frame-does-not-clear-the-accepted-target-set
cases.why: The frame that tells a rider one favourite was refused is a `status` frame arriving **after** the snapshot that names the survivors — the shard sends exactly this pair, `bad_request` / `retryable: false` for the dropped target beside `state: 'live'` for the connection, because `state` describes the connection and `error` describes the thing the message names. A reducer that rebuilt the state literal here and forgot the echo would erase the answer one frame after it arrived, leaving the five working stops and no way to name the sixth. Pinned separately from `a-status-frame-updates-status-and-nothing-else` because that row's subject is `seq` and `etas`, and a port fixing one has no reason to look at the other.

cases.name: a-pong-changes-nothing
cases.why: Liveness, not data — and on Cloudflare it is answered by the runtime without the object waking, so it may not have been produced by our own code at all. `applied: false` is what tells a caller not to repaint.

cases.name: an-unknown-frame-type-is-ignored-not-fatal
cases.why: A frame type added to the protocol after this client shipped. Nothing in this package validates at runtime — the contract imports are types and erase — so an unknown `type` reaches the reducer as an ordinary string on every already-installed client. Ignoring it is the tolerance the wire contract promises; throwing would turn one additive protocol change into a crash on phones we cannot update.

acceptTargets.doc: Which targets can be watched, and which cannot — called by BOTH transports, so a favourite whose id no longer parses is dropped identically by the poll emulator and by the socket, and the caller gets the rejects back so it can say so instead of showing a short list. A silently short list is the same class of dishonesty as a fake countdown. The accepted set is canonical (one entry per stop, sorted, `routeIds` sorted) because it feeds the connect URL, the `subscribe` frame and the shard hash; `rejected` keeps input order because it is a diagnostic a rider reads back. Duplicates merge by UNION, never by dropping one: a dropped duplicate would narrow the subscription while `rejected` stayed empty, so nothing anywhere would say a route had been lost.

cases.name: a-lone-pole
cases.why: The base case, and the shape `stop/[id].tsx` sends: one canonical pole, no narrowing, meaning every route at it.

cases.name: a-merged-place-is-a-valid-target
cases.why: Most interesting stops in the dataset are merged places (ADR-042) and a place id is what a rider's screen holds, so rejecting one would make the feature useless where it matters most. `parseStopOrPlaceId` accepts both shapes; nothing here special-cases the prefix.

cases.name: route-narrowing-is-kept-and-sorted
cases.why: A route-at-stop favourite watches one route, not the whole pole. The ids come back sorted because the accepted set feeds a URL and a frame, and two clients with the same interest must produce the same bytes or they land on different shards.

cases.name: an-unparseable-stop-id-is-rejected-not-dropped
cases.why: The ordinary failure: a favourite saved under an older id scheme, or a hand-edited URL. It comes back in `rejected` so the screen can name it. Returning it silently in neither list is what makes a short list unexplainable.

cases.name: a-place-id-with-one-broken-member-is-rejected-whole
cases.why: A place id with a member dropped denotes a DIFFERENT place, so tolerating the malformed one would subscribe the rider to somewhere they did not ask for. Same rule as `parsePlaceId`'s, reached through it rather than restated.

cases.name: an-empty-route-list-asks-for-nothing-and-is-rejected
cases.why: `routeIds: []` is not 'all routes' — absent means that. An empty array asks for no routes, which is a subscription that can never produce a reading and on screen is indistinguishable from a stop with no buses due. So it is a caller bug, and it is rejected loudly rather than reinterpreted.

cases.name: one-unparseable-route-id-rejects-the-whole-target
cases.why: Narrowing to the ids that happened to parse would quietly change WHICH buses the rider is watching, and the screen would look perfectly normal. The honest answer is to reject the target and say so.

cases.name: a-stop-id-in-the-route-slot-is-rejected
cases.why: The confusion the id grammar is built to make impossible: a stop id has two fields, a route id four, so `KMB:1234` is not a route and `parseRouteId` says so. Pinned because a port using a permissive split would accept it and then filter every reading away.

cases.name: duplicate-narrowed-targets-merge-by-union
cases.why: Favourites can hold two routes at one pole as two rows. Both must be watched — a merge that kept only the first would silently stop watching the second, with nothing in `rejected` to explain it.

cases.name: all-routes-absorbs-a-narrowed-duplicate
cases.why: A union with 'everything' is everything. The Place screen wants the whole pole while Favourites wants one route at it; the wider ask wins, because the narrower one is already contained in it.

cases.name: all-routes-absorbs-a-narrowed-duplicate-in-the-other-order
cases.why: The same result with the arguments swapped — the merge must be commutative, or the accepted set depends on the order a screen happened to assemble its targets in, which is exactly the history-dependence D1 forbids.

cases.name: accepted-targets-are-sorted-by-stop-id
cases.why: Code-point order, no locale. This is what makes two clients with the same interest hash to the same shard: `liveShardFor` takes the lowest id, and 'lowest' has to mean the same thing on every platform.

cases.name: an-empty-request-is-not-an-error
cases.why: A screen with no favourites yet. Two empty lists, not a throw — the caller decides whether to open a socket at all, and it cannot decide that if asking costs an exception.

nextLiveCadenceMs.doc: The shard's adaptive alarm rule. `null` means *do not set an alarm at all*, which is the whole economy of the design: a Durable Object with no alarm and no subscribers hibernates, and a hibernated object accrues no duration charge, while one that keeps ticking to discover nobody is listening pays for every tick plus a metered row write per `setAlarm`. Otherwise the cadence starts at the 45 s floor and widens one step per consecutive unchanged round to the 60 s ceiling. The floor is the measured upstream interval (mean 44.75 s over 4 intervals, 2026-07-30, one KMB route, off-peak — a first measurement, not a characterisation); the ceiling is the vendor's stated refresh. Nonsense inputs fall back rather than producing a NaN alarm nobody can trace.

cases.name: no-subscribers-means-no-alarm
cases.why: The last socket closed. Returning the floor here — or 0 — is the difference between a shard that costs nothing and one that polls upstream for an empty room for ever.

cases.name: an-absent-count-means-no-alarm
cases.why: The caller could not count its sockets (a cold constructor after hibernation, before the socket list is read). Absent is not zero-with-confidence, but the safe answer is the same: no alarm, and the next connection will set one.

cases.name: a-negative-count-is-not-a-count
cases.why: The shape of an arithmetic slip in the caller. Rejected rather than clamped, on the same reasoning as `resolveClientPolicy`: a clamp invents a policy nobody wrote.

cases.name: one-subscriber-and-something-just-changed-polls-at-the-floor
cases.why: The busy case. A pole that just changed is worth asking again promptly, and 45 s is already at the data's own floor — the measured mean interval.

cases.name: one-quiet-round-widens-by-one-step
cases.why: The ramp, first step. Whole seconds by construction: the span is 15 s and the ramp is 3 rounds, so each step is 5 s and no platform has to agree about rounding.

cases.name: two-quiet-rounds
cases.why: The middle of the ramp. Pinned so a port that implemented a doubling or a jump straight to the ceiling fails here rather than silently polling differently.

cases.name: three-quiet-rounds-reaches-the-ceiling
cases.why: The end of the ramp, exactly at the vendor's stated refresh interval. At this cadence the object is hibernated for 50 s of every minute, which is the real reason the slow cadence is cheap.

cases.name: a-long-quiet-stop-never-exceeds-the-ceiling
cases.why: Overnight, when Hong Kong has no live arrivals at all (roughly 01:00–05:30 HKT). The clamp is what stops an unbounded ramp turning into an alarm hours away, which would look identical to a broken shard.

cases.name: an-absent-round-count-is-treated-as-zero
cases.why: A shard that has just woken has no memory of previous rounds — hibernation discards in-memory state. The safe reading is 'assume something changed', i.e. the floor.

cases.name: a-negative-round-count-is-treated-as-zero
cases.why: A counter that went negative is a caller bug; the cadence still has to be a number a `setAlarm` can take, and the floor is the answer that cannot be too slow.

cases.name: a-fractional-round-count-is-floored
cases.why: JSON has no integers, and a caller computing an average of rounds would produce this. Flooring keeps the ramp on its whole-second steps; a port that multiplied by the fraction would emit 52500 ms and no test would ever look at it.

cases.name: many-subscribers-do-not-make-it-faster
cases.why: Forty people watching one pole is the case sharding exists for, and it must not multiply the upstream load — the cadence is a property of the DATA, not of demand. A port that scaled with subscribers would hammer upstream exactly when it matters.

liveReconnectDelayMs.doc: The client's reconnect schedule: `min(maxMs, initialMs · factor^(attempt-1))`, then **half jitter**, so the answer is always inside `[capped/2, capped]`. The rows read as the plain 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 30 s ramp because they pin `jitter: 1`, the band's deterministic top edge. This is arithmetic and not a timer: *when* to try again, the attempt counter and 'reset on a frame, not on an open' stay in `createSocketTransport`, where a test can watch the second attempt happen at the right moment. It is in this corpus because it was a client-layer secret while `packages/ports/src/live-transport.ts` claimed the policy was 'written down once' — in a file naming `URLSessionWebSocketTask` and OkHttp as the iOS and Android implementations, neither of which can read TypeScript. Two failures these rows exist to catch, both silent: an exponent that inverts (a retry *faster* than the initial delay, i.e. a tight loop against a server that has just dropped us) and a jitter that reaches zero (every client back in the same instant, which is the load a restarted shard cannot take).

cases.name: the-first-reconnect-waits-one-second
cases.why: The top of the band on the first attempt: `capped/2 + 1·capped/2` is `capped`, so `jitter: 1` is the deterministic upper edge of the real policy and the rows below read as the plain 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 30 s ramp. Short enough that a connection dropped in a tunnel repairs itself before a rider notices, long enough not to be a tight loop against a Worker that is refusing the upgrade.

cases.name: the-second-attempt-doubles-it
cases.why: Doubling is the whole growth rule, and a port that read `factor · attempt` instead of `factor^(attempt-1)` agrees with the row above and with nothing after it.

cases.name: the-third-attempt-doubles-it-again
cases.why: Where a linear port and an exponential one have visibly parted company.

cases.name: the-fourth-attempt
cases.why: Still under the cap, so this row is about the exponent and nothing else.

cases.name: the-fifth-attempt
cases.why: The last step before the cap binds — 16 s, not yet 30 s. An off-by-one in the exponent shows up here as 32 s clipped to 30 s, which looks correct.

cases.name: the-sixth-attempt-is-capped-at-thirty-seconds
cases.why: `1000 · 2^5` is 32 s and the answer is 30 s. **The cap matters more than the growth:** an uncapped exponential reaches an hour, and a screen left open all afternoon on a bad connection would then take an hour to notice the network came back. 30 s is below the shard's own 45–60 s poll cadence, so a reconnect landing inside one cycle loses no data at all.

cases.name: the-cap-holds-however-long-the-outage-lasts
cases.why: Attempt 12 would be 2048 s uncapped. The row exists because an implementation that capped by clamping the *exponent* rather than the delay overflows quietly in a fixed-width integer on a hand-ported platform.

cases.name: a-jitter-of-zero-is-half-the-capped-delay
cases.why: The bottom of the band. **Half jitter, not full:** every client watching a shard that restarts is disconnected in the same instant, so a fixed delay brings all of them back simultaneously — precisely the load a restarted shard cannot take — while full jitter can produce a near-zero delay, which is the thundering herd again with extra steps. This row is the floor that guarantees it cannot.

cases.name: a-jitter-of-one-half-sits-in-the-middle-of-the-band
cases.why: `4000/2 + 0.5·4000/2`. The row that says the jitter is interpolated across the top half rather than added to the whole delay — a port doing `capped + jitter·capped` also passes both edges.

cases.name: a-jitter-above-one-is-clamped-to-the-top-of-the-band
cases.why: Clamped rather than rejected: a jitter source that overshoots its range is still pointing the right way, and clamping keeps the answer inside the band the policy promises instead of inventing a delay no reviewer has seen.

cases.name: a-negative-jitter-is-clamped-to-the-bottom-of-the-band
cases.why: The dangerous end, and the reason the clamp is not a rejection: an unclamped `-1` would yield a delay of zero, which is an immediate retry into the server that just dropped us.

cases.name: an-absent-jitter-falls-back-to-the-top-of-the-band
cases.why: `capped` — the plain exponential delay the policy would have had without jitter at all, which is the honest answer when the jitter source is the thing that is missing. Never the bottom of the band, because a broken jitter source must not be able to shorten a retry.

cases.name: a-fractional-delay-is-rounded
cases.why: `1001/2 + 0.5·1001/2` is 750.75. Rounded, not truncated, and pinned because a timer handed a fractional millisecond behaves differently on every platform — and because a port using integer division would land on 750 here and agree with every other row in this group.

cases.name: the-zeroth-attempt-is-the-first-attempt
cases.why: A counter that has not been incremented yet. The exponent would be −1, i.e. a *shorter* delay than the initial one — the one arithmetic slip in this expression that produces a tight loop rather than a wrong-but-safe number. Same reasoning as `nextLiveCadenceMs`' guards: a computed number that is not a positive finite value is a misconfiguration, not an aggressive setting.

cases.name: a-negative-attempt-is-the-first-attempt
cases.why: Same guard, from the other side. `2^-4` is a 62 ms retry loop.

cases.name: an-absent-attempt-is-the-first-attempt
cases.why: Absent, rather than nonsense — the ordinary call from a caller that has not tracked failures.

cases.name: a-fractional-attempt-truncates-to-the-earlier-step
cases.why: Floored, so a counter that arrived as a fraction waits the *shorter* legal delay rather than an interpolated one no row in this group describes. 2.9 is attempt 2.

cases.name: an-attempt-below-one-does-not-invert-the-exponent
cases.why: The row the floor-then-clamp order exists for: 0.5 is positive, so a `> 0` guard alone lets it through, and `Math.floor(0.5)` is 0 — the same inverted exponent `the-zeroth-attempt-is-the-first-attempt` catches, reached by a value that guard cannot see.

cases.name: a-supplied-cap-overrides-the-default
cases.why: The three schedule parameters are inputs, not constants, because that is what keeps them testable: this is the shape `createSocketTransport`'s `SocketBackoff` injection produces, and the socket's own suite asserts the same 1 → 2 → 3 → 3 s schedule against it.

cases.name: a-supplied-initial-delay-overrides-the-default
cases.why: `250 · 2^1`. The other end of the same injection point.

cases.name: a-factor-of-one-never-widens
cases.why: A legal constant-delay policy: 1 s for ever. The boundary the guard below is measured against.

cases.name: a-factor-below-one-is-floored-at-one
cases.why: A factor under 1 *shrinks* the delay with every failure, which is a tight loop against a server that has just refused us — the opposite of what a backoff is. Floored rather than replaced by the default, because the caller's intent (do not widen) is legible and honouring it costs nothing.

cases.name: an-unusable-initial-delay-falls-back-to-the-default
cases.why: Zero is not a fast reconnect, it is no reconnect delay at all — `0 · 2^n` stays 0 for ever, so every attempt would retry immediately.

cases.name: an-unusable-cap-falls-back-to-the-default
cases.why: A negative cap would make `Math.min` return it and the delay would be negative — a timer scheduled in the past, i.e. the tight loop again, arrived at from the one parameter whose job is to prevent long waits.

liveShardFor.doc: Which `EtaHub` shard owns a target set (D4): sort the accepted stop ids, hash the lowest with FNV-1a (32-bit), take it modulo the shard count. Clients watching the same places therefore share one upstream poll, which is the case that matters — a stop is hot because many people are looking at it. The CLIENT never computes this: it connects to `/v1/live?targets=…` and the Worker hashes, so a client compiled against a stale shard count cannot silently land somewhere else. The expected numbers below were computed from the FNV-1a specification independently of the TypeScript, so a port that produces a different number has a wrong hash — check the 32-bit wrapping multiply and the unsigned shift first, which are the two places every language differs.

cases.name: one-pole-lands-on-a-stable-shard
cases.why: The base case. The number itself is arbitrary; that it never changes is the property — every reconnect must reach the same object or the shard's cached snapshot is useless.

cases.name: the-same-interest-set-hashes-the-same-whatever-order-it-is-given
cases.why: Two screens assemble the same two favourites in opposite orders. If the hash depended on input order they would open two sockets to two shards and poll the same poles twice — the exact duplication sharding exists to prevent.

cases.name: only-the-lowest-id-decides-the-shard
cases.why: Adding a higher-sorting target leaves the shard where it was — which is what lets a rider add a favourite without moving their socket. Pinned as the same value as the first row so a port that hashed the whole concatenated set fails here.

cases.name: an-added-lower-target-does-move-the-shard
cases.why: The honest cost of the rule, pinned rather than hidden: adding a target that sorts below the current lowest re-homes the connection, so the client reconnects and the new shard polls from cold. Bounded by the shard count, and only for partially overlapping sets — but real, and a reader should see it stated.

cases.name: route-narrowing-does-not-affect-the-shard
cases.why: The shard owns POLES, not routes: two clients at one pole watching different routes must share the poll. Hashing the narrowing too would split them for no benefit.

cases.name: an-unparseable-target-does-not-affect-the-shard
cases.why: Rejected targets are gone before the hash — `acceptTargets` runs first — so one stale favourite cannot re-home a rider's whole connection. A port that hashed the raw input would move them to a different shard the moment a saved id went bad.

cases.name: no-targets-hashes-the-empty-string
cases.why: Deterministic rather than clever, and documented rather than accidental: this is the FNV-1a offset basis modulo the shard count. A connection with nothing to watch should be refused before it reaches this function — the shard it would land on is not a meaningful answer, and this row exists so nobody discovers that by reading a NaN.

cases.name: a-single-shard-collapses-everything
cases.why: The dev configuration, and the one that proves the modulo is applied rather than the raw hash returned.

cases.name: a-shard-count-of-zero-falls-back-to-the-default
cases.why: `x % 0` is NaN, and a NaN shard id becomes the Durable Object name "live-NaN" — a real object that silently collects every client and serves them one shared poll set. The fallback turns a config slip into a working system rather than an invisible one.

cases.name: a-fractional-shard-count-falls-back-to-the-default
cases.why: The shape of a shard count read from an environment variable and divided. A fractional modulus produces a fractional shard, which names an object nobody intended — so only a positive integer is honoured.

cases.name: a-place-id-hashes-as-the-string-it-is
cases.why: A merged place id is a long string with `+` and `:` in it and is hashed verbatim, member ids and all. It is NOT decomposed into its poles: the id is what the rider saved and what the connect URL carries, so it is what must decide the shard.

cases.name: a-wider-shard-count-spreads-the-same-id
cases.why: The same pole with 64 shards instead of 8. Pinned so a port cannot pass every row above by returning a constant, and so the arithmetic is checked against two moduli.

liveSocketUrl.doc: Derive the socket URL from the configured API base URL (D5), so Wave 5 adds no new required environment variable — dropping in the real domain stays one variable per renderer. String manipulation only, no URL parser: this is the rule three platforms would each get subtly wrong in a different way, and the one that matters is forgetting `https:`→`wss:`, which ships a rider's location and favourites in cleartext, works perfectly in dev against `http://localhost:8787`, and shows no symptom anywhere. An input with neither scheme is passed through unchanged with the path appended, deliberately: the input is a configured variable, and rewriting something we do not recognise would replace a visible misconfiguration with an invented URL.

cases.name: https-becomes-wss
cases.why: THE row. A port that got this wrong would work in every dev environment and encrypt nothing in production.

cases.name: http-becomes-ws
cases.why: The other half of the mapping, and the reason it cannot be 'always wss': a local Worker has no certificate, so a hard-coded `wss:` would make dev unusable and invite somebody to special-case localhost in a screen.

cases.name: the-local-worker-default
cases.why: Verbatim the default both renderers compile in (`EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL` / `VITE_API_URL`), so this row is what `pnpm dev` actually produces — including the port.

cases.name: a-trailing-slash-is-stripped
cases.why: An env var a human typed. Without stripping, the path becomes `//v1/live`, which some routers treat as a different path — and nobody would look twice at the env file.

cases.name: several-trailing-slashes-are-stripped
cases.why: The same slip, twice. Pinned separately because a port using `removeSuffix("/")` once passes the row above and fails this one.

cases.name: a-base-path-survives
cases.why: An API mounted under a prefix — a reverse proxy, or a preview deployment. The path is appended to whatever base was configured rather than replacing it.

cases.name: an-explicit-wss-override-passes-through
cases.why: The escape hatch D5 keeps for a separate socket host: `EXPO_PUBLIC_LIVE_URL` / `VITE_LIVE_URL` already carry a ws scheme, and it must survive untouched rather than being mangled by a second mapping.

cases.name: an-explicit-ws-override-passes-through
cases.why: Same, unencrypted, for a local socket tier. Falls out of the pass-through rule rather than needing a case of its own — which is the argument for the pass-through.

cases.name: a-scheme-less-base-passes-through-with-the-path-appended
cases.why: A misconfiguration, and it stays visible: `api.example/v1/live` is not a socket URL and fails loudly at connect. Inventing a scheme would guess — and guessing `wss:` for a host that only speaks plain HTTP is a failure nobody could read off the config.

cases.name: an-empty-base-yields-a-relative-path
cases.why: An unset environment variable read as `''`. The result is the path alone, which a browser resolves against the page origin — occasionally useful, always visible, never a silent connection to the wrong host.

cases.name: an-uppercase-scheme-is-not-recognised
cases.why: URL schemes are case-insensitive, and this rule matches lower case only. Recorded rather than handled: an unconverted `HTTPS://` URL is still accepted by the WebSocket constructor (the URL spec maps http/https to ws/wss), so the failure mode is benign, whereas silently lower-casing a URL a human typed is a change we cannot justify from this function. If it ever needs handling, this row is where the decision goes.

applyLiveEtasToStopDetail.doc: Merge a set of live readings into the `StopDetail` a Place screen holds, replacing the ETAs and nothing else. Two rules carry the weight. **The reading list is the complete current set, not a patch**: a row with no matching reading becomes `null`, never its previous value, which is the same honesty `gone` exists for — and the corollary is the footgun, so pass the session's readings, never a delta's `changed`, or every other row on the screen blanks. **Every non-ETA field survives**: `stop`, `members`, and each row's `route`, `stopId` and `fare` are all read by the screen, and the value written back has to stay the shape the HTTP fetch produced or ADR-058's persisted cache replays a payload the screen cannot render. **A row whose exact service-type variant upstream did not publish takes the soonest reading for its own rider line at its OWN pole** (WP5-9): a board publishes whichever variant is running and a row names one, so the exact pair alone drops real arrivals. That fallback index is built by `dedupeEtas` and keyed by `etaBoardingKey` — the same normalisation and the same key the wire keys on, never a second rule — and it never crosses a pole, so a rider is never shown a bus at a kerb it is not coming to.

cases.name: a-live-reading-replaces-the-row-it-belongs-to
cases.why: The base case. Matching is by the `(stopId, routeId)` pair — the row's member pole and the row's route — because a place's rows each depart from their own kerb (ADR-042).

applyLiveEtasToNearby.doc: Merge live readings into the `NearbyStop[]` the Nearby list holds. **This is the one list in the module that is NOT in `(stopId, routeId)` order, and the exception is load-bearing**: `stopCardView` caps a card by taking the first `maxRows` readings, so this order decides WHICH buses a rider sees, and `/v1/nearby` serves them soonest-first. A canonical id order here would silently turn "the next three buses" into "three routes whose ids sort first" — a change no test would catch and every rider would. So: soonest first, readings with no arrival last, and a total tiebreak on `(stopId, routeId)` because a comparator returning 0 would leave the result to the platform's sort stability (guaranteed in TypeScript, unspecified in Swift). Readings are matched to a place through its member poles, since an `Eta.stopId` is always a pole while a `NearbyStop.stop.id` may be a merged `P:` id.

cases.name: readings-reach-a-merged-place-through-its-member-poles
cases.why: THE matching row. The place id is `P:CTB:001965+KMB:548…` and the readings are stamped with the poles. A port comparing `stop.id` with `eta.stopId` directly leaves every merged place — which is most of the interesting ones — with an empty card, and the list still renders.

narrowEtasToRoutes.doc: The `routes=` narrowing, as one rule rather than as two filters (WP5-7). It runs in the edge's `stopEtas` for `/v1/etas/:id?routes=` and in the poll emulator for a target that named routes — the batch endpoint carries no per-id route list, because `,` is a legal `idchar` and there is no safe delimiter for a nested one, so the client narrows one hop after the batch answers while the `EtaHub` shard goes on narrowing server-side. Written twice the two would eventually disagree about a route id that no longer parses or about the empty list, and identical listener output on both engines is exactly what the live-rounds corpus asserts. It narrows READINGS and never failures, and it preserves the caller's order rather than canonicalising.

cases.name: absent-routes-narrows-nothing
cases.why: THE CONTROL, and the branch every healthy round takes. `undefined` means "every route at this stop" — the ordinary case — so an implementation that treated it as an empty allow-list would blank every arrival in the app while satisfying every other row here.

cases.name: an-empty-list-narrows-nothing-rather-than-everything
cases.why: "I named no routes" is not "I want no readings" — the caller that means the latter unsubscribes. `acceptTargets` rejects a `routeIds: []` target outright, so this branch is reachable only from `?routes=` with nothing after it, which is a caller mistake; serving the whole board is the harmless direction and blanking the screen is not.

cases.name: keeps-only-the-named-routes-in-the-order-given
cases.why: The ordinary narrowing, and the order matters: this is a filter over a list whose caller has already decided the order — `stopArrivals` serves soonest-first and that ordering is a rider-facing decision. Re-sorting here would silently overwrite it.

cases.name: narrows-by-route-across-every-pole-of-a-place
cases.why: A place is N boarding poles (ADR-042) and one line can board at two of them (WP5-9), so narrowing to a route must keep BOTH of that route's readings. An implementation keyed on the (pole, route) pair would drop the sibling kerb, which is the defect WP5-9 exists to prevent arriving from a new direction.

cases.name: a-route-nobody-lists-narrows-to-nothing
cases.why: An empty result is the honest answer to "show me a route that is not here", and it is NOT the same as the empty-list case above. A rider watching one route at a stop that has stopped running it should see no arrivals rather than every arrival.

liveTargetsKey.doc: A stable string identifying WHICH SUBSCRIPTION THIS IS, so a live hook's effect can depend on a string instead of on an array (WP5-7). It exists because of a request storm rather than for tidiness: a `WatchTarget[]` is a fresh array on every render, the subscription's own readings re-render the screen, and `subscribe` fires a round immediately — so an array dependency makes a subscription resubscribe on its own output, unboundedly, one HTTP request per turn. The key is over the ACCEPTED set, so two orderings of one set are the same subscription (which is what a Nearby list produces as a rider walks a few metres) and an unwatchable id falls out for free; an EMPTY STRING therefore means "nothing here can be watched". `|` is the only separator because it is the one structural character absent from every stop and route id, and each target contributes an arity field (`*` for all routes, else the count) so that no two distinct accepted sets can spell one key.

cases.name: one-target-all-routes
cases.why: THE CONTROL and the ordinary case: absent `routeIds` means every route, spelled `*`, so the key of the commonest subscription in the app is stable and short.

cases.name: nothing-watchable-is-the-empty-string
cases.why: The condition a hook needs before it opens anything at all. `acceptTargets` rejects an id that does not parse, so a screen holding only stale favourites must not subscribe — and a key that was non-empty for a set with nothing in it would have it open a connection watching nothing.

cases.name: two-orderings-of-one-set-are-one-key
cases.why: THE SECOND CONTROL, and the whole reason the key runs over the accepted set. A Nearby list reorders as a rider walks a few metres; keyed on the array as given, every such reorder would tear down the subscription and fire an extra round inside the same window — which breaks the request-count property WP5-7 exists for.

cases.name: a-duplicate-id-does-not-change-the-key
cases.why: `acceptTargets` merges two targets for one stop by union, so asking twice is one subscription. A key built from the input would resubscribe when a caller deduplicated its own list.

cases.name: a-narrowed-target-carries-its-arity-and-its-routes
cases.why: The count is what keeps each target self-delimiting under one separator. Without it `{P:KMB:A+KMB:B}` and `{P:KMB:A, routes:[KMB:B]}` — two different subscriptions — would spell the same key, because `+` separates the members of a place id and `:` is inside every id. That collision is a failure to resubscribe, which is silent.

cases.name: a-place-id-with-a-plus-is-not-mistaken-for-a-route-list
cases.why: The collision the arity field prevents, from the other side: a merged place id contains `+`, and this key must be different from the narrowed single-pole target above. Both rows are needed — either alone passes an implementation that used `+` as its route separator.

sameFailures.doc: Is this round's failure set news? The predicate that lets a frame carry `failed` without making every round a repaint (WP5-14, ADR-081). The failure set moves independently of the readings — a kerb can start refusing, or recover, while every reading a subscriber holds stays byte-identical — so "an unchanged round is silent" needs this to know whether the round was unchanged. Both engines ask it, so a disagreement here is two engines sending a different number of frames for one outage. `stopId`, `error.code` and `error.retryable` are compared; **`error.message` is NOT**, because it is prose that embeds whatever the upstream said and a wording that varied between two rounds describing one outage would make every round news. Both lists are canonically ordered by `stopId`, so the comparison is element-wise.

cases.name: two-empty-sets-are-the-same
cases.why: THE CONTROL, and the state almost every round is in. An implementation that returned false here would send a data frame every single round and undo the delta protocol.

cases.name: the-same-pole-failing-the-same-way-is-not-news
cases.why: The round-two-of-an-outage case, and the one this predicate exists for: the kerb is still refusing and no reading changed, so the round must stay silent and the client must keep the marker it already has.

cases.name: a-pole-that-started-refusing-is-news
cases.why: Round one of an outage. Without this the card could not say "we could not ask" until some *reading* happened to change, which during an outage is exactly what stops happening.

cases.name: a-pole-that-recovered-is-news
cases.why: THE ROW THE ACCEPTANCE NAMES: "a recovered kerb's marker clears within one round". A recovery often changes no reading a client can see — the fresh board can repeat what `retainFailedPoles` was already holding — so if this returned true the marker would outlive the recovery by a whole cadence.

cases.name: a-different-pole-failing-is-news
cases.why: Same count, different kerb. A predicate that compared only lengths would call this unchanged and the card would name the wrong kerb — or, on Nearby, attribute the outage to the wrong card entirely.

cases.name: the-same-pole-with-a-different-code-is-news
cases.why: A timeout becoming an outright refusal is a different fact about the same kerb, and `code` is what a caller branches on. It costs one frame and buys an accurate error.

cases.name: the-same-pole-turning-permanent-is-news
cases.why: `retryable` is the field that decides whether a background client keeps asking (ADR-064), so a change in it must reach the client even though nothing else about the failure moved.

cases.name: a-message-that-changed-is-not-news
cases.why: THE SECOND CONTROL, and the one that keeps the predicate useful. The message embeds the upstream's own words; if it carried a timestamp or a retry count it would differ every round, every round would be news, and the delta protocol would be pointless. Same argument as `COMPARED_FIELDS` excluding `observedAt`.

unionFailures.doc: One round's failure set from the per-target lists it came back with: deduplicated by pole, sorted by `stopId` in code-point order (WP5-14, ADR-081). A round is N targets and each answers with its own `failed`, so the frame needs the union — and it has to be built identically on both engines or the two send different bytes for identical upstream behaviour, which is the property ADR-074's corpus asserts. First occurrence wins on a duplicate, and the lists arrive in accepted-target order, so "first" is the earliest target that reported the pole. `sameFailures` relies on the ordering, so the two rules are only correct together.

cases.name: no-failures-anywhere-is-an-empty-set
cases.why: THE CONTROL, and the shape of every healthy round. Note the input is a list per target, so this is three targets that all answered — not an empty round.

cases.name: one-target-with-two-refusing-kerbs
cases.why: A place is N boarding points (ADR-042) and an upstream board call is per point, so one target can contribute two entries. The result is sorted, which is what makes the frame byte-identical on both engines.

cases.name: two-targets-sharing-a-pole-collapse-to-one-entry
cases.why: THE ROW THAT MATTERS, and it is reachable rather than theoretical: a rider can watch a merged place AND one of its own member kerbs at once — a Nearby card is keyed on the place, a favourite on the kerb (ADR-062) — and the batch endpoint answers about both. Two entries for one kerb would make the wire claim two outages, and `sameFailures` would then see a length change where nothing changed.

cases.name: the-first-target-to-report-a-pole-wins
cases.why: The dedupe keeps the EARLIEST entry, not the last, and the difference is observable when two targets describe one kerb differently — a place-level fan-out that timed out and a pole-level one that got a 502. Both engines walk their targets in accepted order, so "earliest" is the same entry on each; last-wins would also be deterministic but would depend on target order in the opposite direction, which is the sort of thing two hand-ports get differently.

cases.name: a-target-that-answered-contributes-nothing
cases.why: THE SECOND CONTROL. The common mixed round: one place refusing, one fine. An implementation that emitted a placeholder for the healthy target would mark every card on the screen incomplete.

routeWatchName.doc: Which `EtaHub` object owns a route watch. The route id IS the identity, so every rider on one route shares one object and one upstream round — and an id that is not a route id must mint no object at all, because it arrives from a query string and `route-<anything>` would be a real Durable Object (the `live-NaN` hazard `liveShardFor` records). `null` in a fixture is the language’s absent value.

cases.name: the-reverse-direction-is-a-different-route-and-a-different-object
cases.why: Both bounds are watched independently and their poles barely overlap, so sharing one object would union two rounds for no benefit.

cases.name: a-stop-id-is-not-a-route-id
cases.why: The id arrives from a query string, so the caller must be able to answer 400 — see the `live-NaN` hazard on `liveShardFor`.

cases.name: text-that-is-not-an-id-at-all-mints-no-object
cases.why: The whole point of the validation: `route-<script>` would be a real Durable Object.

nextRouteRoundMs.doc: When a route watch asks again, aligned to the ROUTE’s own publish clock rather than to the CDN’s TTL. The upstream advertises `max-age=45` but its data moves on a ~60 s cycle at a per-route second of the minute, so polling on the advertised number re-reads a publish it already had about one round in four (measured 2026-08-10, proposals/05). Four arms: no publish to align to; one that did not advance with a readable `age` (the one question `45 − age` genuinely answers — when does THIS entry turn over); the same without an age; and one that did advance.

cases.name: a-fresh-publish-aims-just-after-the-next-one
cases.why: E22 published at :12–:13 in the measurement, so a round at 21:29:20 that saw 21:29:12 should next ask at 21:30:15 — the period plus the margin, 55 s away. Deliberately not a multiple of any constant, so this answer can only come from the arithmetic.

cases.name: the-first-round-of-a-watch-has-nothing-to-compare-against
cases.why: No previous publish is not the same as an unadvanced one: the first round of a watch has news by definition, so it aligns rather than retries.

cases.name: a-stale-copy-waits-for-that-entry-to-turn-over
cases.why: The publish did not advance and the response carried `age: 30`, so this entry expires in 15 s — the one question `45 − age` genuinely answers. 18 s with the margin, which is distinct from the blind retry.

cases.name: a-nearly-expired-stale-copy-is-floored-rather-than-chased
cases.why: age 44 leaves 1 s, plus 3 s of margin, which is under the floor. The floor is what stops a turnover race becoming a tight loop.

cases.name: a-stale-copy-with-no-age-to-read-falls-back-to-the-blind-retry
cases.why: Same situation, measurement missing. Kept as its own answer so a guess and a measurement do not read alike in a schedule.

cases.name: a-nonsense-age-is-no-age-at-all
cases.why: A negative or unusable header falls back to the blind retry rather than computing a delay from it — the same call `resolveClientPolicy` makes about unusable numbers.

cases.name: a-publish-older-than-the-one-before-it-is-also-no-news
cases.why: Two CDN edges can disagree, so a round can be handed something older. It is still nothing new.

cases.name: an-out-of-service-route-reports-no-publish-at-all
cases.why: Citybus 962 returned zero rows outside its morning hours. There is no phase to align to, so tick at the period.

cases.name: an-unreadable-timestamp-is-absent-rather-than-zero
cases.why: Treating it as epoch zero would clamp to the maximum wait on garbage; treating it as absent ticks at the period.

cases.name: a-round-that-took-so-long-the-next-publish-has-been-and-gone
cases.why: The target is already past. A slow round must not earn a negative delay — the floor is what stops a tight loop.

cases.name: a-skewed-clock-cannot-park-a-watch-for-an-hour
cases.why: A timestamp far in the future would otherwise compute an enormous delay. The ceiling is the answer.
